citations.quote: Paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct provides that distributors should not offer any gifts (other than a discount of fees or charges) in promoting a specific investment product or a particular type of investment product to a client.

If gifts are offered in such a way that they are linked to a particular type of investment product, such as certain types of funds or funds offered by certain fund houses, then such gifts will be bound by this requirement as investors may be distracted from the unique features and risks of such particular funds3.

Even where the guaranteed returns offered would not constitute a “structured product” under the SFO, distributors are reminded to have regard to paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct in offering such returns or other incentives in promoting SFC-authorised funds, as they may be considered a gift that should not be offered to investors.

Typically, the “guaranteed returns” in such cases comprise: (i) the actual return of the relevant fund(s) invested by the investor (ie, fund return); and (ii) a top-up return to make up the difference between the fund return and the guaranteed rate of return offered by the distributor.

reading.distinction: A single offer-level Boolean such as 'includes a discount' would hide the difference between an excepted fee discount and a separate potentially prohibited gift. A Boolean limited to promotion of a named fund would also omit product-type promotion, including funds from particular fund houses. Finally, absence of structured-product classification does not remove the need to classify the component under the gift restriction.

reading.distinction: The prior component model abstraction.ea48395ee1fc075eb75b04b4 describes the distributor as the provider and places provider_is_distributor in scope. citations.quote: Intermediaries who distribute these funds (distributors) have been offering additional returns or other incentives that may divert the client’s focus from properly considering the risks and features of the underlying funds.

Typically, the “guaranteed returns” in such cases comprise: (i) the actual return of the relevant fund(s) invested by the investor (ie, fund return); and (ii) a top-up return to make up the difference between the fund return and the guaranteed rate of return offered by the distributor.

Even where the guaranteed returns offered would not constitute a “structured product” under the SFO, distributors are reminded to have regard to paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct in offering such returns or other incentives in promoting SFC-authorised funds, as they may be considered a gift that should not be offered to investors.

Paragraph 3.11 of the Code of Conduct provides that distributors should not offer any gifts (other than a discount of fees or charges) in promoting a specific investment product or a particular type of investment product to a client.

If gifts are offered in such a way that they are linked to a particular type of investment product, such as certain types of funds or funds offered by certain fund houses, then such gifts will be bound by this requirement as investors may be distracted from the unique features and risks of such particular funds3.

reading.distinction: A single offer-level Boolean such as 'contains a discount' would hide separate benefits and could incorrectly extend the discount exception to an accompanying gift. A Boolean limited to promotion of a named fund would also miss promotion of a fund type or funds from a particular fund house. Finally, 'guaranteed return' cannot stand in for 'gift': the source distinguishes fund return from distributor top-up and uses qualified gift-classification language.

questions.question: No prior models were supplied for a missing-schema challenge. Inspection of the proposed model identifies component boundaries, product-type linkage, client relationships and offer timing as material distinctions. The supplied evidence supports retaining them in one model rather than inventing a rival interpretation.

A combined-offer conclusion requires a complete component inventory and an assessment of every component. For a known finite inventory, component prohibition results can be joined with (or ...). The present expression answers only the component-level question and cannot establish that an incompletely inventoried offer contains no prohibited gift.

The supplied text does not define an exhaustive test for gift status or resolve every boundary between discounts and additional returns. These classifications remain professional-judgment inputs, not assumed truths.
The section 103 structured-product restriction is separate and is not evaluated here. Absence of a prohibited gift under this model does not resolve that restriction or other requirements.

No prior models were supplied for a missing-schema challenge. The present review identified consequential component, product-type and offering-time distinctions and incorporated them into one proposal; the supplied text does not justify a second rival reading.

A whole-offer decision requires a complete inventory and assessment of all components. For a known finite inventory, a disjunction of component prohibition results could identify at least one prohibited component. The supplied fragment cannot quantify over an unspecified inventory. What is the complete component inventory?
The source supplies no exhaustive definition of a gift or fee/charge discount, and the referenced FAQ is not included. Those classifications require professional judgment and remain unassigned.
No facts about an actual offer or applicable effective dates were supplied. This proposal supplies an interpretation and predicate, not an evaluated decision or legal approval.
Both prior models already preserve component separation, product-type promotion and offering-time assessment. The source does not support inventing additional temporal or product-scope rivals.

The offeror/provider distinction is consequential only if 'provider' in the prior model means funder or fulfiller. If it means offeror, the proposed correction clarifies the vocabulary rather than establishing a different legal reading.

The words 'any gifts' require coverage of every relevant component before a negative whole-offer conclusion. A known finite inventory permits a disjunction of component results; an unspecified inventory cannot be quantified over in the supplied expression fragment. What is the complete component inventory?

The source does not supply exhaustive gift or discount definitions, the referenced FAQ answer, or a complete attribution test for third-party benefits. These remain judgment questions rather than assigned truths.
No actual offer facts are supplied. Legal completeness, equivalence of the prior models and compliance with separate restrictions remain unestablished.
